Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 33 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives / SIL Cameroon archive entry 96002). Appendix A: Tone Orthography Proposal (December 2015).
tone_statements.quote: There are four main tone patterns (or melodies) for nouns in Chufieʼ: H, L, HL, LH. Although there are eight words with LHL and eleven words with HLH tone pattern, these seem to be exceptions[12], and are rare in comparison to the other patterns (H: 164 L: 183 HL: 128 LH: 125). [...] Verbs: Lexical tone in verbs has a very high functional load, because verbs have two tone classes, H and L and there are many minimal pairs (50+ pairs when looking at 580 basic verbs). [...] There are five grammatical categories which consist solely of a tonal morpheme (no segmental information exists with any of these morphemes in any context).
tone_statements.locator: Appendix A 'Tone Orthography Proposal (December 2015)', pp. 29-30; '[12]' marks footnote call 12 in the original; also sec. 3 Tone, p. 17

tone_statements.citation: Ben-Shalom, Dorit. 1994. The Tones of Nchufie Verbal Inflection. In Hilda Koopman and Murat Kural (eds.), Aspects of Nchufie Grammar (UCLA Occasional Papers in Linguistics 14), pp. 47-56. Los Angeles: UCLA Department of Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: This paper is concerned with the tonal patterns of inflected monosyllabic verbs in Nchufie. We assume that Nchufie verbs fall into two types: Ø-tone and L-tone verbs. Verbs of the same class behave identically in terms of the tones of their verbal inflection. The inflections of L-tone verbs differ from those of Ø-tone verbs in that they have an extra L (low) tone. [...] We are assuming that none of the tones in (1) and (2) are default tones. In other words, the tones of verbal inflection all originate as lexical tones of the relevant verbs, moods, and tenses.

sources.citation: Hamm, Cameron and Valerie Hamm. 2007. A Phonological Sketch of Bafanji (Chufie'). Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. iii+52 pp.
sources.note: Nothing: no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence' in the whole text. Section 5 'Tone' (pp. 26-29): three surface level tones H, M (suspected downstepped H), L plus Rising, Falling, Low-falling contours; lexical tone on monosyllabic roots, Low-toned noun prefixes, two tonal verb classes, tense distinguished by tone. p. 3: 'Tone carries a heavy functional load.' p. 18: monomoraic syllables 'pronounced more quickly and with less emphasis than bimoraic syllables' (weight, not stress).

sources.quote: This paper is concerned with the tonal patterns of inflected monosyllabic verbs in Nchufie. We assume that Nchufie verbs fall into two types: Ø-tone and L-tone verbs. Verbs of the same class behave identically in terms of the tones of their verbal inflection. The inflections of L-tone verbs differ from those of Ø-tone verbs in that they have an extra L (low) tone. sources.note: Analyses the tonal patterns of inflected monosyllabic verbs; verbs fall into two classes, toneless (Ø-tone) and L-tone; inflectional tone patterns (future, hortative, present/past, perfect, progressive, imperative) arise from lexical tones of verbs, moods and tenses, none being default tones; L of L-tone verbs surfaces on the final syllable, as the second half of a HL fall, or shifts onto an object pronoun; object-pronoun tones depend on verb class, tense/mood and pronoun. Koopman's introduction (p. 4-5) summarises it the same way.
